subject: Running CFA binary variables return low factor loading

messages.author: ff0d489e75490dc3
messages.subject: Running CFA binary variables return low factor loading
parts: Good morning, guys. I'm running a SEM using DWLS estimator in R. I'm wondering when I tested for validity, two of my construct consist of Likert-type questions (to measure behavior) and the other two consist of 8 binary items each (to measure knowledge, each 1 represents a correct answer), the problem is when i test for validity and reliability the factor loadings of Likert-type items is relatively high (0.7+) while the binary is extremely low (0.1-0.3). Is this a good way to measure the “Knowledge” construct? If so, why is the loadings of binary items are so so low?

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Running CFA binary variables return low factor loading
parts:
Phuct,
You need to consider whether these are raw or standardized loadings.  It is also relevant whether you are treating the non-binary items as ordinal, or as continuous.   Raw loadings are sensitive to the standard deviations of the items (and latent variables).  In a model with thresholds, this applies to the scaling of the unobserved continuous item variable.

These things can get a little tricky because you want to evaluate the validity of the observed scores, not the unobserved continuous item variables.  You may want to examine the estimated thresholds for the binary items to see if they are extreme.  It may also be helpful to examine some classical item analysis indices like the correlations between the binary items and the corresponding adjusted sum scores (i.e., sum score minus the item score) and the univariate frequency tables for the items.

Sometimes with knowledge tests, the domain of knowledge is very large.  As a result, each item in the sample of items may have a relatively low correlation with knowledge of the overall domain and with other items in the domain.  This is particularly likely if the test is designed to include items with a wide range of item difficulties.  Nonetheless, in a long enough test, positive manifold can still produce a reliable test.  The probability of a person with high knowledge getting most of the items wrong on a very short test may be non-negligibly high but the same probability for a longer test may become very small.

Keith
